e: note:'Ras Tanura and Juaymah are inside the Persian Gulf. Every laden VLCC must clear Hormuz before crossing the Indian Ocean to Malacca. Saudi Arabia is China\'s largest single crude supplier and the dominant contributor to its Malacca structural dependency.'

e: note:'Basra Oil Terminal and Khor Al-Amaya are inside the Persian Gulf. Mandatory Hormuz transit. Iraq\'s crude runs long-haul across the Indian Ocean and through Malacca to east coast Chinese ports at Qingdao and Ningbo-Zhoushan.'

e: note:'Ahmadi and Mina Abdullah terminals are deep inside the Persian Gulf. Mandatory Hormuz transit for all Kuwait Export Crude destined for China. Kuwait\'s share has held at around 6 to 7 percent.'

e: note:'Mina Al Fahal and Duqm terminals are on the Gulf of Oman, seaward of Hormuz. Ships enter the Arabian Sea directly without transiting the Persian Gulf. No Hormuz exposure. Oman crude still transits Malacca to reach Chinese east coast ports. Hormuz and Malacca are independent risks for Oman volumes - a key distinction in chokepoint risk decomposition.'

e: note:'Malaysian crude from Sabah and Sarawak (Labuan, Bintulu) loads in the South China Sea and routes via Malacca to Chinese east coast refineries. Not a Gulf producer at all - included here because it transits Malacca only. Malaysia also functions as a re-export and blending hub; some volumes attributed to Malaysia in bilateral data may originate from sanctioned suppliers.'

e: note:'Cabinda, Girassol, and CLOV crude loads on VLCCs that exit the Atlantic, round the Cape of Good Hope eastward, and cross the Indian Ocean. CDM Fix-10 confirms West Africa to Asia crude routes via Lombok Strait, not Malacca. A Malacca closure has no effect on Angola supply to China.'

e: note:'Bonny Light and Qua Iboe follow the same Cape of Good Hope route as Angola. VLCCs transit Lombok Strait into the South China Sea from the east, bypassing Malacca entirely. Also represents smaller volumes from Congo, Gabon, and Equatorial Guinea on the same routing.'

e: note:'Santos basin and pre-salt FPSO loadings. Atlantic-origin VLCCs at laden draught cannot transit the Panama Canal. The route is eastward around the Cape of Good Hope - not Cape Horn, which is a longer westward passage essentially unused for VLCC crude to China. Lombok Strait entry to South China Sea. Also includes Colombian and Guyanese Atlantic loadings.'

e: note:'Gulf of Mexico loadings (Mars, Thunder Horse, Shenandoah). VLCC class vessels at laden displacement are too large for the Panama Canal. Route is Cape of Good Hope eastward to Lombok. No Malacca transit. Includes some additional Atlantic Americas volumes (Trinidad, Ecuador Atlantic-coast loadings).'

e: note:'East Siberia Pacific Ocean pipeline delivers crude to Kozmino terminal near Nakhodka on Russia\'s Pacific coast. Tankers cross the Sea of Japan directly to Qingdao, Dalian, and Ningbo-Zhoushan. No maritime chokepoint on the supply path. Kazakhstan is landlocked and ships no crude by sea; it is absorbed in this node for completeness. Neither supply source has any maritime chokepoint exposure.'

e: note:'The Strait of Hormuz is the mandatory exit for all crude loaded inside the Persian Gulf. Minimum navigable width approximately 3.2 km; no alternative maritime route for laden VLCCs. Gulf-inside producers (Saudi Arabia, Iraq, UAE, Kuwait) represent 44% of China\'s seaborne crude import value and all transit Hormuz. A Hormuz closure would be the first interruption point for this supply before it even reaches Malacca. Oman loads seaward of Hormuz and does not transit it.'

e: note:'The Malacca Strait narrows to approximately 2.8 km. There is no viable alternative maritime route for laden VLCCs from the Indian Ocean into the South China Sea. A closure event would strand crude equivalent to 55.8% of China\'s annual seaborne import value with no short-run diversion. This is the correct number for the Malacca Dilemma calculation. Gulf-inside producers (44%) face Hormuz and Malacca sequentially. Oman (8%) and Malaysia (4%) face Malacca only.'

e: sub:'20.6% · via Cape of Good Hope'

note:'The Lombok Strait (between Bali and Lombok, Indonesia) is a deep-water chokepoint handling VLCC traffic from the Indian Ocean that approaches China from the east. West African and Americas cargoes round the Cape of Good Hope, cross the Indian Ocean, and transit Lombok into the South China Sea. A Malacca closure does not interrupt this supply path - and vice versa. These flows account for 20.6% of China\'s seaborne crude; they are the source of the inflated "80%" figure when combined with the Malacca total.'

A Malacca closure does not interrupt this supply path - and vice versa. These flows account for 20.6% of China\'s seaborne crude; they are the source of the inflated "80%" figure when combined with the Malacca total.

e: note:'Russian ESPO crude from Kozmino (Pacific coast) transits no maritime chokepoint between origin and Chinese east coast terminals. Kazakhstan crude to China travels the Atyrau-Alashankou overland pipeline with no sea leg at all. This 23.6% is structurally insulated from any maritime closure - Malacca, Lombok, or otherwise. Most analyses of the Malacca Dilemma substantially understate this figure.'

e: note:'China is the world\'s largest crude importer by volume, receiving approximately 11 to 12 mb/d of seaborne crude in 2022. Primary east coast receiving terminals: Qingdao (Shandong independent refiners), Ningbo-Zhoushan (the world\'s largest port by cargo tonnage), Dalian (CNPC), and Tianjin. The east coast refinery geography is the structural driver of Malacca dependency - every barrel arriving from the Indian Ocean must pass through either Malacca or Lombok.'
